title: Our Father, once more
hookLine: the prayer from the first week, now with five years in it
tomorrow: which word did a whole crowd shout with their hands in the air?

lines: I NEED, I'M SORRY, I HOPE.
cards: Journal pages fill up with I: I need, I'm sorry, I hope. Now count the I's in the prayer this path met in its first week. In Matthew, in the King James, it says our, us, we.
Not once does it say I, me or my. Pray it alone in an empty room and it still won't let you go singular. So whose Father is this?

teach.b: Here's how Matthew gives the opening: "Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven." In the first week these were new words.
Now there are five years in them, and the first one holds the rest. Our.

teach.h: HAVE WE NOT ALL ONE FATHER?
teach.b: The prophet Malachi asked it long before: "Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?" One father, one family, and his very next question is why people deal falsely with their own brothers.
Christians differ on how wide that our reaches, but the prayer itself never shrinks to my. Now a neighbor who says it too.

teach.h: AVINU MALKEINU: OUR FATHER, OUR KING.
teach.b: In the Days of Awe, around the Jewish new year and Yom Kippur, Jewish prayer repeats Avinu Malkeinu, our Father, our King, line after line asking for mercy. Two traditions, one word in common: our Father.

Christians pray the Lord's Prayer as the prayer Jesus taught, the one they call God's Son; Jews don't pray it as his prayer or share that belief about him, and Avinu Malkeinu has its own words and its own season.
Neither is a copy of the other. Both say our.
Churches pray this one in different ways too: some end with For thine is the kingdom, some say trespasses for debts, some sing it. The words barely change. The people saying them do.

how: Christians pray the Lord's Prayer in worship and on their own, Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant alike, said or sung, with some churches ending on 'for thine is the kingdom' and some saying 'trespasses' where others say 'debts'.

o: the prayer Jesus taught, which says us, never me
a Christmas carol about Joseph, Jesus's father
a prayer only priests may say during a service

have we not all one father?

s: the Lord's Prayer, as Matthew gives it in the King James, never says I, me or my
it says our, us and we all the way through.
Avinu Malkeinu is the Hebrew name for the Lord's Prayer
it's a Jewish prayer of its own, our Father, our King, prayed in the Days of Awe.
every church ends the Lord's Prayer with the same words
some end with 'for thine is the kingdom'; some say trespasses, others debts.

games.q: your Jewish neighbor says her family prays "our Father, our King" at the new year. what's a fair reply?
o: "so it's the same prayer as ours, just in Hebrew."
"we both call God our Father; ours is the prayer Jesus taught."
"then your family should pray the Lord's Prayer too."
games.why: Avinu Malkeinu and the Lord's Prayer share the words our Father. they're different prayers from different seasons, and neither is a copy of the other: shared ground, honest difference.

practice: If you pray, say the Lord's Prayer slowly, one line to a breath, and stop wherever a word holds you. If you don't, let the words pass through your mind and count each us and our.

wordCard.voice: Our Father. The prayer from the first week, word for word the same, with five years now folded into its first word.

orig.note: Greek: Father of ours, the opening words in Matthew 6:9.

carryVoice: The line for today: our father, never my father in this prayer. Sleep well, or good morning.
